newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: CAPE TOWN PLANS ITS OWN "SILICON VALLEY".
newsitem.headline: CAPE TOWN PLANS ITS OWN "SILICON VALLEY".

text.p: Detailed planning has started on an ambitious 3.5 billion rand research and industrial park near Muizenberg on the False Bay coast modelled on California's Silicon Valley.

Backed by a consortium including insurance giant Norwich Life and Anglovaal's Grinaker Properties and Projects, the 200 hectare Capricorn Science and Manufacturing Park will be developed over the next 20 years with the first phase, covering 65 ha, expected to be completed by the end of 1998.
Another backer is British-based Science Research Parks Limited, a subsidiary of National Leasing and Finance.

"It's a bold initiative, but South Africa has to change its mindset. It has to become international in its attitude and unless we take those kinds of steps, we will always remain a third rate nation," chairman Rodney Squire-Howe told Reuters after a presentation on the project.
Squire-Howe said shareholders had already invested between five and six million rand in researching the project and would raise between 50 and 60 million rand to market and service the first stage.

The low-rise park will cater for offices, research facilities, light industry, education and training and will include a beachfront leisure zone and housing. Companies will be able to buy plots to develop or lease buildings, which will be sited next to man-made lakes and landscaped gardens.

Capricorn managing director Raven Naidoo said the aim would be to encourage high tech research and development in areas such as telecommunications and information technology, and create up to 35,000 new jobs.
Announced four years ago, the project has been held up because of delays in getting the Cape Town City Council to upgrade a major road linking the park site to the city centre and airport.
"It's all systems go for Capricorn," Naidoo said. "Professional teams have been appointed and environmental impact studies and rezoning applications are underway."
